verses.translation_literal: To the leader, with stringed music, a psalm to/of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung with the strings: a psalm of David.
verses.directors_commentary:
This line is not part of the song. It is the label on the scroll, a performance instruction handed to the person in charge of the Temple musicians. In the Hebrew text it counts as verse 1, which is why every verse number in this psalm runs one ahead of the KJV, which prints it as an unnumbered heading.

The KJV leaves two terms in Hebrew-looking English: 'chief Musician' for lamnaTzeach and 'Neginoth' for bingiNot. The first is the one 'set over' the singers and players (Ibn Ezra, Radak); the root is also used for those who oversee work on the House of the LORD (Ezra 3:8, as Rashi points out), so 'choirmaster' is a job title, not a flourish. The second is plural for stringed playing; the ASV and YLT translate it, as I do. The final word, ledaVid, uses the preposition lamed, which can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to' David. It does not by itself settle who wrote it, and the commentators differ on the occasion (Absalom's revolt for Radak and Meiri; a famine for Malbim).

philological_notes.note: The one set over the musicians; the same root gives 'oversee' in Ezra 3:8. Rashi links it to those who press forward in the Temple service; Ibn Ezra says it is the official over the singers. Metzudat Zion derives it from 'to prevail' by raising the voice. Choirmaster is the traditional sense, but the root's other meaning ('victory', 'forever') is not excluded.
Plural of neginah, 'playing on strings'. Ibn Ezra offers three possibilities: a melody with two tunes, an instrument, or many tunes in Israel. Radak says it is a named instrument or style.

verses.translation_literal: In my calling, answer me, God of my righteousness! In the tight place you made room for me. Be gracious to me and hear my prayer.
verses.translation_dramatic: When I call, answer me. You are the God who knows my cause is just. You have found me in the tight place before and led me out into open ground. Be gracious to me now, and hear what I am praying.
verses.directors_commentary:
The man praying is hemmed in. The Hebrew picture is spatial: tzar is the 'narrow place', a ravine or a squeezed throat, and the verb hirChavta is its opposite, 'you made it wide'. The singer remembers a time when God gave him room, and uses that memory as grounds to ask again. The Hebrew keeps that image; the KJV's 'enlarged me' tries, and the ASV's 'set me at large' is closer. The BBE flattens it to 'make me free from my troubles'.

Play 'God of my righteousness' as a legal claim. In a world without private courts, an innocent man had only the right to appeal to the highest judge. Radak reads it as 'you know that right is on my side and the injustice on theirs'. The KJV's 'Hear me' for the first verb is also a softening: the Hebrew is 'answer', a call for action, not just a hearing. The verb 'hear' is saved for the last clause.

philological_notes.note: 'God of my righteousness': the God who vindicates me, or the God who is the source of my being in the right. Ibn Ezra reads God as the first cause that shows my righteousness; Radak reads elohim as 'judge', citing Exodus 22:8. Meiri notes the possibility of a superfluous yod ('God of righteousness').

'You made wide': the opposite of tzar, 'narrow'. Rashi reads it of earlier days; Radak as a prophetic perfect with future force. The image of 'wide space' for salvation is standard in the psalms (compare Ps 18:20 [Hebrew 18:20], 'he brought me out into a broad place'), which is my own parallel and I give no source.

verses.translation_literal: Sons of man, until what [time is] my glory for disgrace? [Until when] will you love emptiness, [will] you seek a lie? Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: You, sons of men, men of rank: how long will you drag my honor down into the dirt? How long will you cling to what is hollow, and go hunting for a lie? Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the singer turns from God to the people who are slandering him. Radak notes that 'sons of ish' is deliberately not the common 'sons of adam': ish is a man of standing, so these are leaders (he pairs the two words as in Ps 49:3). The KJV's 'sons of men' erases that difference. Aim it at the great and the well placed; this is not a crowd.

The verse is built on three accusations. 'My glory' is his honor and standing; the KJV's 'turn my glory into shame' supplies a verb that the Hebrew lacks ('until when my glory for disgrace?'). Radak says that, as king, he is being shamed by his own subjects. 'Emptiness' (riq) is something with nothing in it, a hollow plan; 'lie' (kazav) is what fails like a dried-up stream, as Radak and Meiri say, citing Isaiah 58:11. The KJV's old word 'leasing' (archaic English for falsehood) hides this. Then comes Selah, the first of two in this psalm: a pause, whose exact meaning is unknown.

philological_notes.note: Men of standing, as opposed to bnei adam, the common crowd. Radak makes the distinction with Psalm 49:3, and Metzudat Zion glosses ish as 'great and important', citing 1 Samuel 26:15. Rashi instead reads it as 'sons of the patriarchs', who are called ish.
A lie, in the sense of something that fails and cannot be relied on (like a dried-up spring). Radak and Meiri tie it to 'waters that do not fail' in Isaiah 58:11.

A musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning, perhaps a pause or a lifting of voice. It occurs twice in this psalm, at the end of Hebrew 4:3 and again at the end of 4:5, and nowhere else in it. Malbim uses these two markers to divide the psalm into three parts.

verses.translation_literal: And know that YHWH has set apart a faithful one for himself. YHWH hears when I call to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Know this, all of you: the LORD has marked out a loyal man as his own. The LORD hears me when I call out to him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The singer now answers his accusers with a flat statement of fact. The divine name repeats, 'YHWH ... YHWH', one at the start of each half, like two hammer blows. The KJV says 'the Lord' both times, where the Hebrew has the name itself.

The hard word is hifLah. The root means to 'make distinct' (the same verb as in Exodus 9:4, where the LORD sets Israel's cattle apart from Egypt's, so Radak). Rashi simply glosses it hivdil, 'separated'. The word chasid is not 'godly man' in the loose KJV sense. Radak defines it as one who does good beyond the line of the law, as David did to Saul, and the singer claims the title for himself (Meiri compares Ps 86:2). So this is a king's answer: I was picked out, and you cannot undo it. The BBE ('see how the Lord has made great his mercy for me') reads a different root and loses the claim of distinction.

philological_notes.note: 'Made distinct, set apart': the same verb is used for the LORD separating Israel's livestock from Egypt's in Exodus 9:4 (Radak). Rashi glosses it hivdil, 'separated'. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'set apart' and quotes 'and I will set apart on that day' (Exodus 8:18; his text labels it chapter 32).
A man of loyal kindness, from chesed. Radak: one who acts beyond the strict requirement of the law, as David did to Saul (1 Sam 24:18). Meiri notes that David calls himself chasid, as in Ps 86:2.

verses.translation_literal: Tremble, and do not sin. Speak in your heart upon your bed, and be silent. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Tremble, if you must, but do not sin. When night comes and you lie down, say it quietly to your own heart, and then be still. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a night scene. The order of the verbs is the instruction: shake, but do not sin; talk, but only inward; then fall silent. The KJV's 'stand in awe' makes the first verb gentler than it is. rigZu is a bodily word, to quiver or be shaken, and it can be fear or anger; Radak and Rashi take it as the fear of God, as in Deut 2:25, and Ibn Ezra the same. Keep it physical.

The KJV 'commune with your own heart' is pleasant but it replaces a plain 'say in your heart'. For the Hebrews the heart is the place of thinking, and Radak notes that 'saying' can mean thought (Isa 47:8). The bed is where the day's busyness falls away (Radak, Metzudat David), so the words land in a quiet room. 'Be silent' (domu) is not a calm word either; Radak sets it with the sea hushed in Psalm 107:29 and the sun standing still in Joshua 10:13. It means: stop moving. The BBE's 'have bitter feelings' invents a sentiment the Hebrew does not state.

philological_notes.note: To quiver or shake, with fear or with anger; the root covers both. Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as fear of God, Radak comparing Deut 2:25.
To be still or silent, of voice or of motion. Radak gathers the examples: Job 29:21, Psalm 107:29, Joshua 10:13, and Habakkuk 2:19 (the 'silent stone').

verses.translation_literal: Sacrifice sacrifices of righteousness, and trust in YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bring the offerings that are right, and put your trust in the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the speaker turns to ritual, and the line is short and flat on purpose. The verb and its noun share a root, zivchu zivchei, so the Hebrew sounds like 'sacrifice sacrifices'; the KJV 'Offer the sacrifices' loses the echo and the repeated sound. Keep it as a rhythmic pair.

'Sacrifices of righteousness' can mean offerings brought correctly and with a clean conscience. Radak sets them against 'the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination' (Prov 21:27): a sacrifice is worth something only if the giver turns from the wrong. Rashi, Metzudat David and the Targum go further and read it as 'make your deeds righteous and God will count it as an offering', which is not an actual sacrifice at all. The text does not choose, so play it as a call to the believers in the audience to act rightly in the Temple and outside it. The last clause uses 'trust in' with el, 'toward', as Radak notes, where 'on' (al) is more usual.

philological_notes.note: 'Sacrifices of righteousness': offerings made rightly, or righteous conduct counted as an offering. Radak contrasts it with Prov 21:27; Rashi, Metzudat David and the Targum read it as making one's deeds righteous.

verses.translation_literal: Many are saying, 'Who will show us good?' Lift up upon us the light of your face, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: So many around me are asking, 'Who will show us anything good?' But I ask for something else: LORD, lift the light of your face over us.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood opens up. 'Many' voices ask a worried, grasping question: who will show us something good? Commentators disagree about who: Radak takes it as the rebels hoping for the king's fall; Rashi and Metzudat David take it as people who want wealth; Malbim as people in famine hoping for rain. Whichever you pick, the speakers are looking for a tangible 'good', and the singer answers with a prayer for presence instead.

'Light of your face' is the language of a king's or a god's favor: a shining face means welcome, a hidden one means refusal. The verb is nesah, an odd form of 'lift' (Radak, Ibn Ezra), and Rashi hears in it nes, a banner raised on a pole, so the face is lifted like a signal flag over the camp. It echoes the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:25-26, which is my own parallel. The KJV 'countenance' is stiff and now means little more than 'expression'; the Hebrew word is simply 'face'. The BBE reverses the sense altogether: 'the light of his face has gone from us' turns a plea into a complaint.

philological_notes.note: An unusual imperative of 'lift', with h for aleph (Radak, Ibn Ezra). Rashi and Metzudat Zion connect it to nes, a banner raised on a pole, as in Isa 62:10.

'The light of your face': the favor of the one whose face shines on you. Meiri reads it as light for our darkness; Radak as the nearness of God in the world to come, as against the worldly good the many want.

verses.translation_literal: You have put joy in my heart, from [the] time [that] their grain and their new wine have become many.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have set a joy inside me, deeper than theirs, deeper than the gladness of the harvest, when the threshing floors are full and the new wine is pouring.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew verb is natatah, 'you have given, set', so the joy is a gift placed inside the man, not something he has earned. The KJV 'put gladness' is accurate here. Stage it as quiet and interior, set against the loud rejoicing of the harvest.

The harvest is concrete. dagan is grain, the staple crop, and tirosh is new wine, fresh grape juice and must rather than aged wine; both were the marks of a good year, when a family would eat. The KJV renders dagan as 'corn', which in the English of its day meant any grain and not maize, and 'wine' for tirosh blurs the distinction.

The unresolved phrase is me'Et: 'from the time' (YLT) or 'more than the time' (KJV, ASV, with the comparative min). Metzudat David takes the comparative: my joy in my lot is greater than that of those many who rejoice when their grain and wine abound. Radak and Meiri read it differently: they repay him evil for good, rejoicing at his trouble, while he rejoiced in their prosperity whenever he saw their grain and wine multiply. Ibn Ezra reports an emendation of the word order and finds no need for it. I follow the comparative in the dramatic layer; play either as a contrast between his gift and their gain.

philological_notes.note: 'From the time' (temporal) or 'more than the time' (comparative min). The comparative is in KJV and ASV and in Metzudat David; the temporal is in YLT and fits Radak and Meiri, for whom David rejoiced in their prosperity. Ibn Ezra cites Judah ibn Bal'am for reversing the word order and rejects the need.
New wine, the fresh juice of the grape harvest, rather than matured wine (yayin). Metzudat Zion glosses it as the juice of grapes.

verses.translation_literal: In peace together I will lie down and [I will] sleep, for you, YHWH, alone, to security, will make me dwell.
verses.translation_dramatic: In peace I lie down, and at once I sleep. For you, LORD, you alone, let me live in safety.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends where it began, in a bed, but now the man is calm. The verbs are 'I will lie down and I will sleep', two short beats, and the Hebrew word yachdav, 'together', ties them tightly: he lies down and sleeps in the same breath. Metzudat David reads it as 'immediately, one after the other', because the anxious sleeper cannot drop off at once. Rashi and Radak read 'together' as with the people: peace with his enemies. Both readings are allowed by the Hebrew, and I take the first in the dramatic layer.

The last line is ambiguous. levaDad, 'alone', can belong to YHWH (you alone) or to the man (me alone, secure without an army), as Rashi says with Deut 33:28 ('Israel dwells in safety, alone'). The KJV 'only' sides with the first. Then comes laVetach, 'to security': the word 'safety' hides nothing, but it is a state, not a place. Note the cluster of sounds: shalom, eshkevah, ishan, vetach. It is the sleep of a man who has no fear of the night.

philological_notes.note: 'Together' or 'at once'. Rashi and Radak read it as together with the people; Metzudat David as one right after the other; Ibn Ezra as the many, with him among them.
'Alone', 'by yourself'. It may modify YHWH ('you alone') or the speaker ('me alone'). Rashi and Metzudat Zion compare Deut 33:28, 'Israel dwells in safety, alone'; Radak takes it with YHWH.
